On the Redundancy of Timestep Embeddings in Diffusion Models

José A. Chávez Affiliation: Independent Researcher, Lima, Peru E-mail josechavez.ie@gmail.com
Abstract

Diffusion models rely heavily on explicit timestep embeddings to modulate the denoising process across various noise scales. In this work, we challenge the necessity of these temporal signals by analyzing their impact on U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures. Beyond empirical evidence, we provide a theoretical framework demonstrating that, under certain conditions, the global minimizer of the diffusion training objective can be achieved without explicit timestep conditioning. Our findings reveal a surprising robustness when timestep embeddings are completely removed. Extensive ablation studies on the CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets show that these time-agnostic models can maintain high structural fidelity and even surpass their conditioned counterparts in competitive metrics, including FID, precision, and recall. Our analysis suggests these architectures can implicitly infer noise scales from the corrupted input under specific assumptions, rendering explicit temporal conditioning redundant. This study challenges long-standing temporal conditioning paradigms and paves the way for more efficient and structurally focused generative architectures.

Keywords: 
timestep embeddings

1 Introduction

Diffusion Models [23] have shown significant success in generative modeling, synthesizing high-fidelity data through a gradual denoising process [6, 19, 2, 21]. These models rely heavily on timestep embeddings, which serve to encode temporal information to adjust the noise removal level at each step. This information is typically injected via feature map addition or modulation across the model architecture.

Recently, transformer architectures have emerged as a powerful alternative to convolutional backbones in diffusion models. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) [17], based on the Visual Transformer architecture [4], provide several key advantages over traditional U-Net architectures. Chief among these is scalability; DiT demonstrates superior performance as model size and computational power increase, showing strong correlations between GFLOPs and sample quality. This allows for superior performance in high-resolution image generation and large-scale datasets. Furthermore, transformers excel at modeling long-range dependencies due to their self-attention mechanism, enabling better coherence in image generation by capturing relationships across distant regions of an image. DiTs outperform traditional U-Net backbones on ImageNet [3] at 512×512512\times 512 and 256×256256\times 256 resolution.

Regardless of the architectural backbone chosen—be it a U-Net or a DiT—current implementations fundamentally depend on a mechanism to inject the temporal signal or the noise scale. Although the importance of timestep embeddings is widely accepted, there has been limited investigation into their actual necessity. In this work, we challenge the conventional wisdom by exploring whether these temporal signals are truly indispensable for diffusion model architectures to effectively learn the denoising process. We conduct a rigorous ablation study on both U-Net and DiT architectures, systematically removing explicit timestep conditioning to evaluate the impact on sample quality and structural fidelity. Our empirical results reveal a surprising robustness in these time-agnostic models, which can maintain high performance even without explicit temporal signals.

Our contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We conduct a rigorous ablation study on the effect of timestep embeddings across both convolutional (U-Net) and transformer-based (DiT) diffusion architectures.

  2. 2.

    We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis that timestep signals can be functionally redundant under certain conditions, as the model can implicitly recover the noise scale directly from the corrupted input.

2 Background

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM) [6] are latent variable models of the form pθ(𝐱0):=∫pθ(𝐱0:T)d𝐱1:Tp_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0}):=\int p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0:T})d\mathbf{x}_{1:T}, where 𝐱1,…,𝐱T\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{T} are latent variables in the same sample space as 𝐱0∼q⁡(𝐱0)\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim q(\mathbf{x}_{0}). The forward process is defined as a Markov chain that gradually adds Gaussian noise to the data:

q(𝐱1:T∣𝐱0):=∏t=1Tq(𝐱t∣𝐱t−1),\displaystyle q(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0}):=\prod^{T}_{t=1}q(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t-1}), (1)

where the true posterior q⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱0):=𝒩⁡(𝐱t,α¯t​𝐱0,(1−α¯t)​𝐈)q(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0}):=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{t};\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0},(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\mathbf{I}) is parametrized by a time-dependent scalar α¯t∈{α¯1,…,α¯T}\bar{\alpha}_{t}\in\{\bar{\alpha}_{1},\dots,\bar{\alpha}_{T}\}. After a re-parameterization we can write:

𝐱t:=α¯t​𝐱0+1−α¯t​ϵ,\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{t}:=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, (2)

where ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}).The reverse process is defined as a Markov chain:

pθ(𝐱0:T):=pθ(𝐱T)∏t=0Tpθ(𝐱t−1∣𝐱t).\displaystyle p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0:T}):=p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{T})\prod^{T}_{t=0}p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}). (3)

2.1 The Training Process

In the standard DDPM framework [6], a neural network ϵθ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta} processes two inputs: the corrupted image 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and the discrete timestep t∈{0,1,…,T}t\in\{0,1,\dots,T\}. The objective function is to predict the ground-truth noise ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon} added to the original image 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} in Eq. 2 by minimizing the following loss function:

ℒ⁡(θ)=𝔼𝐱0,ϵ,t​[‖ϵ−ϵθ​(𝐱t,t)‖2].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t}[||\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)||^{2}]. (4)

Although minimizing ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta) is standard practice, the absolute dependence of tt as an explicit input remains an open question.

We can obtain the global minimizer of ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta) with respect to ϵθ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta} using the total expectation law:

ℒ⁡(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta) =𝔼𝐱t,t[𝔼ϵ|𝐱t,t[||ϵ−ϵθ(𝐱t,t)||2∣𝐱t,t]].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t},t}[\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t}[||\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)||^{2}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t]]. (5)

The global minimizer can be obtained by analyzing the inner expectation for each fixed 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and tt. If we define 𝐲:=ϵθ​(𝐱t,t)\mathbf{y}:=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) and ϕ(𝐱t,t):=𝔼ϵ|𝐱t,t[||ϵ−𝐲|𝐱t,t||2]\phi(\mathbf{x}_{t},t):=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t}[||\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}_{t},t||^{2}], we can obtain the global minimizer 𝐲∗\mathbf{y}^{*} of ϕ⁡(𝐱t,t)\phi(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) by setting the gradient of ϕ⁡(𝐱t,t)\phi(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) with respect to 𝐲\mathbf{y} to zero:

𝟎\displaystyle\mathbf{0} =−2𝔼ϵ|𝐱t,t[ϵ∣𝐱t,t]+2𝐲∗\displaystyle=-2\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t]+2\mathbf{y}^{*}
∴ϵθ∗​(𝐱t,t)\displaystyle\therefore\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{*}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) =𝔼ϵ|𝐱t,t[ϵ∣𝐱t,t].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t]. (6)

Now, to understand the role of the timestep tt in the training process, we need to analyze how it is injected into the architecture. In practice, DDPM injects the timestep as a positional encoding (pe):

𝐡:=𝐡+ffn​(pe​(t)),\displaystyle\mathbf{h}:=\mathbf{h}+\text{ffn}(\text{pe}(t)), (7)

where ffn is a feedforward network (ffn) and 𝐡\mathbf{h} is the input of each convolutional layer in the U-Net architecture. This process is repeated for each convolutional layer in DDPM [6].

DiT [17] instead, integrates the temporal conditioning mechanisms through an Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaIN) [18].

2.2 The Sampling Process

During the sampling process, given the noise predicted by ϵθ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}, DDPM uses it to predict the uncorrupted image 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}:

𝐱0​(θ)=1α¯t​(𝐱t−1−α¯t​ϵθ​(𝐱t,t)).\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{0}(\theta)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)\right). (8)

As stated in DDPM, 𝐱t−1\mathbf{x}_{t-1} can be predicted using 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} and 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}:

𝐱t−1=α¯t−1​(1−αt)1−α¯t​𝐱𝟎​(θ)+αt​(1−α¯t−1)1−α¯t​𝐱t+1−αt​𝐫,\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{t-1}=\frac{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}(1-\alpha_{t})}{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x_{0}}(\theta)+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1})}{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{t}+\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}}\mathbf{r}, (9)

Similarly, DDIM [24] computes first 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} to estimate 𝐱t−1\mathbf{x}_{t-1}.

3 The Redundancy of Timesteps in the Loss Function

Given that samples 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} from the train data distribution q⁡(𝐱0)q(\mathbf{x}_{0}) and Eq. 2 are fulfilled, we can express Eq. 4 as:

ℒ⁡(θ)=𝔼𝐱0,ϵ,t​‖ϵ−ϵθ​(α¯t​𝐱0+1−α¯t​ϵ,t)‖2.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t}||\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t)||^{2}. (10)

Then, using Tweedie’s Formula, we can predict the true posterior mean of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}:

𝔼⁡[α¯t​𝐱0∣𝐱t]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}] =𝐱t+(1−α¯t)​∇𝐱t​log⁡p⁡(𝐱t)\displaystyle=\mathbf{x}_{t}+(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p(\mathbf{x}_{t}) (11)

Here, ∇𝐱t​log​p​(𝐱t)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p(\mathbf{x}_{t}) represents the score function [8]. Following the derivation presented in [15], we can use Eq. 2 to formalize the connection between the ground-truth noise and the score function:

𝐱t−1−α¯t​ϵ\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon} =𝐱t+(1−α¯t)​∇𝐱t​log⁡p⁡(𝐱t)\displaystyle=\mathbf{x}_{t}+(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p(\mathbf{x}_{t}) (12)
∴ϵ\displaystyle\therefore\boldsymbol{\epsilon} =−1−α¯t​∇𝐱t​log⁡p⁡(𝐱t).\displaystyle=-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p(\mathbf{x}_{t}). (13)

Thus, the loss function in DDPM [6] is equivalent to the loss function used in noise conditional score networks [25]. Intuitively, the score function gives a measure of how to move 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} in the data space to maximize its log-probability. Thus, Eq. 10 tries to predict the opposite direction of the score function scaled by 1−α¯t\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}. In other words, the network ϵθ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta} is trained to predict the noise that drives 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} away from the data manifold.

Theorem 3.1

Let 𝐱t=α¯t​𝐱0+1−α¯t​ϵ\mathbf{x}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon} be a corrupted sample with an implicit noise scale α¯t∈(0,1)\bar{\alpha}_{t}\in(0,1), where 𝐱0∼q⁡(𝐱0)\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim q(\mathbf{x}_{0}) and ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}). Let ϵθ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta} be a neural network trained to minimize the time-agnostic loss function

ℒT​A​(θ)=𝔼𝐱0,ϵ,t​[‖ϵ−ϵθ​(α¯t​𝐱0+1−α¯t​ϵ)‖2]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{TA}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t}[||\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon})||^{2}]

Then:

  1. 1.

    The global minimizer ϵθ∗\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{*}_{\theta} of ℒT​A​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{TA}(\theta) satisfies ϵθ∗=𝔼⁡[ϵ∣𝐱t]\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{*}_{\theta}=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}].

  2. 2.

    The global minimizer can be determined by the implicit noise scale α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} and the score function ∇𝐱t​log​p​(𝐱t)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p(\mathbf{x}_{t}).

  3. 3.

    If there exists a measurable map μ:ℝd→(0,1)\mu:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to(0,1) such that μ⁡(𝐱t)=α¯t\mu(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\bar{\alpha}_{t}, then

    ϵθ∗=𝔼[ϵ∣𝐱t]=𝔼[ϵ∣𝐱t,t].\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{*}_{\theta}=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t].
Proof

By the law of total expectation, we can express ℒT​A​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{TA}(\theta) as:

ℒT​A​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{TA}(\theta) =𝔼𝐱t​[𝔼ϵ|𝐱t​[‖ϵ−ϵθ​(𝐱t)‖2∣𝐱t]].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}[\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}}[||\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})||^{2}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}]].

Similar to the derivation of the global minimizer in 6, we have:

ϵθ∗​(𝐱t)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{*}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) =𝔼ϵ|𝐱t​[ϵ∣𝐱t]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}]

Now, we take the conditional expectation with respect to 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} on both sides of Eq. 2:

𝔼ϵ|𝐱t​[ϵ∣𝐱t]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}] =𝐱t−α¯t​𝔼​[𝐱0∣𝐱t]1−α¯t\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbf{x}_{t}-\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}]}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}

Then, we use Eq. 11 to express the global minimizer ϵθ∗\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{*}_{\theta} of ℒT​A​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{TA}(\theta) in terms of the score function:

ϵθ∗​(𝐱t)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{*}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) =−1−α¯t​∇𝐱t​log⁡p⁡(𝐱t).\displaystyle=-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p(\mathbf{x}_{t}).

Since μ⁡(𝐱t)=α¯t\mu(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\bar{\alpha}_{t}, we can define the conditional distribution p⁡(α¯t∣𝐱t)p(\bar{\alpha}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) as a Dirac delta distribution centered at μ⁡(𝐱t)\mu(\mathbf{x}_{t}) because α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} is deterministic given 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}. Consequently, the conditional expectation can be written as:

𝔼ϵ|𝐱t​[ϵ∣𝐱t]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}] =∫𝔼ϵ|𝐱t,α¯t[ϵ∣𝐱t,α¯t]δ(α¯t−μ(𝐱t))dα¯t\displaystyle=\int\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\bar{\alpha}_{t}}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\bar{\alpha}_{t}]\delta(\bar{\alpha}_{t}-\mu(\mathbf{x}_{t}))d\bar{\alpha}_{t}
=𝔼ϵ|𝐱t,α¯t[ϵ∣𝐱t,α¯t]|α¯t=μ⁡(𝐱t)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\bar{\alpha}_{t}}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\bar{\alpha}_{t}]\bigg|_{\bar{\alpha}_{t}=\mu(\mathbf{x}_{t})}

Thus 𝔼ϵ|𝐱t[ϵ∣𝐱t]=𝔼ϵ|𝐱t,α¯t[ϵ∣𝐱t,t]\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}]=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\bar{\alpha}_{t}}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t] as there exists a bijection between α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} and the timestep tt. ∎

Theorem 3.1 shows that the global minimizer of the time-agnostic loss function ℒT​A​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{TA}(\theta) is proportional to the score function ∇𝐱t​log​p​(𝐱t)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p(\mathbf{x}_{t}). Moreover, if there exists a measurable mapping μ:ℝd→(0,1)\mu:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to(0,1) such that μ⁡(𝐱t)=α¯t\mu(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\bar{\alpha}_{t}, the global minimizer of ℒT​A​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{TA}(\theta) is equivalent to the global minimizer of the standard loss function ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta) in 6. Thus, the time signal tt can be disregarded by the network as long as it can implicitly infer α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} from the corrupted input 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}.

Now, we need to prove the existence of the measurable mapping μ:ℝd→(0,1)\mu:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to(0,1) such that μ⁡(𝐱t)=α¯t\mu(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\bar{\alpha}_{t} in order to show that the global minimizer of ℒT​A​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{TA}(\theta) is equivalent to the global minimizer of ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta).

Theorem 3.2

Let 𝐱t=α¯t​𝐱0+1−α¯t​ϵ\mathbf{x}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon} be a corrupted sample on an unknown scale α¯t∈(0,1)\bar{\alpha}_{t}\in(0,1), where

  1. i

    𝐱0∼q⁡(𝐱0)\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim q(\mathbf{x}_{0}) and ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) are independent, and 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is observable.

    𝐱0,ϵ∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

If ‖𝐱0‖2d→𝑃C\frac{||\mathbf{x}_{0}||^{2}}{d}\xrightarrow{P}C for some positive constant C≠1C\neq 1. Then, there exists a sequence of measurable mappings {μd:ℝd→(0,1)}d=1∞\{\mu_{d}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to(0,1)\}_{d=1}^{\infty} such that μd​(𝐱t)→𝑃α¯t\mu_{d}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\xrightarrow{P}\bar{\alpha}_{t} as d→∞d\to\infty.

Proof

Since ‖ϵ‖2∼χ2​(d)||\boldsymbol{\epsilon}||^{2}\sim\chi^{2}(d), we have ‖ϵ‖2d→𝑃1\frac{||\boldsymbol{\epsilon}||^{2}}{d}\xrightarrow{P}1 as d→∞d\to\infty. Moreover, 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} and ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon} are independent, thus 𝔼⁡[𝐱0T​ϵ]=0\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}^{T}_{0}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]=0, and we can express 𝔼⁡[(𝐱0T​ϵ)2∣𝐱0]\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{x}^{T}_{0}\boldsymbol{\epsilon})^{2}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0}] as follows:

𝔼⁡[(𝐱0T​ϵ)2∣𝐱0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{x}^{T}_{0}\boldsymbol{\epsilon})^{2}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0}] =‖𝐱0‖2\displaystyle=||\mathbf{x}_{0}||^{2}
∴𝔼⁡[(𝐱0T​ϵ)2]\displaystyle\therefore\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{x}^{T}_{0}\boldsymbol{\epsilon})^{2}] =𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[(𝐱0T​ϵ)2∣𝐱0]]=𝔼⁡[‖𝐱0‖2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{x}^{T}_{0}\boldsymbol{\epsilon})^{2}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0}]]=\mathbb{E}[||\mathbf{x}_{0}||^{2}]

P⁡(|𝐱0T​ϵd|>δ)≤1d​𝔼​[‖𝐱0‖2d]/δ2\displaystyle P\left(\left|\frac{\mathbf{x}^{T}_{0}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}{d}\right|>\delta\right)\leq\frac{1}{d}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{||\mathbf{x}_{0}||^{2}}{d}\right]/\delta^{2}

as follows:

Therefore, by assumptions of the theorem, we have:

Since h−1​(h⁡(α¯t))=α¯th^{-1}(h(\bar{\alpha}_{t}))=\bar{\alpha}_{t}, we have the following convergence in probability:

h−1​(Hd​(𝐱t))→𝑃h−1​(h⁡(α¯t))=α¯t.\displaystyle h^{-1}(H_{d}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\xrightarrow{P}h^{-1}(h(\bar{\alpha}_{t}))=\bar{\alpha}_{t}.

If we define μd​(𝐱t):=h−1​(Hd​(𝐱t))\mu_{d}(\mathbf{x}_{t}):=h^{-1}(H_{d}(\mathbf{x}_{t})), we obtain μd​(𝐱t)→𝑃α¯t\mu_{d}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\xrightarrow{P}\bar{\alpha}_{t} as d→∞d\to\infty ∎

In practical settings, image data are digitally represented with bounded intensity values (e.g., normalized to [−1,1][-1,1] or [0,1][0,1]). Consequently, the components of 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} are bounded, which immediately implies the existence of uniformly bounded fourth moments. In particular, there exists a constant M>0M>0 such that 𝔼⁡[𝐱0,i4]≤M​ for all ​i∈{1,…,d}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{x}^{4}_{0,i}\right]\leq M\text{ for all }i\in\{1,\dots,d\}. Moreover, since ‖𝐱0‖2≤m2​d||\mathbf{x}_{0}||^{2}\leq m^{2}d for some finite constant m>0m>0, it follows that 𝔼⁡[‖𝐱0‖2d]\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{||\mathbf{x}_{0}||^{2}}{d}\right] is also bounded in standard image datasets.

While natural images exhibit significant local correlations, the dependencies between individual pixels tend to decay rapidly with spatial distance. Thus, under the assumption of a weak dependence condition such that:

∑i<j|Cov​(𝐱0,i2,𝐱0,j2)|=O⁡(d),\displaystyle\sum_{i<j}|\text{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{0,i}^{2},\mathbf{x}_{0,j}^{2})|=O(d),

Then,

Var​(∑i=1d𝐱0,i2)\displaystyle\text{Var}\left(\sum^{d}_{i=1}\mathbf{x}^{2}_{0,i}\right) =∑i=1dVar​(𝐱0,i2)+2​∑i<jCov​(𝐱0,i2,𝐱0,j2)\displaystyle=\sum^{d}_{i=1}\text{Var}(\mathbf{x}^{2}_{0,i})+2\sum_{i<j}\text{Cov}(\mathbf{x}^{2}_{0,i},\mathbf{x}^{2}_{0,j})
≤d​M+O⁡(d)=O⁡(d).\displaystyle\leq dM+O(d)=O(d).

Let C:=𝔼⁡[‖𝐱0‖2d]=1d​∑i=1d𝔼⁡[𝐱0,i2]C:=\mathbb{E}[\frac{||\mathbf{x}_{0}||^{2}}{d}]=\frac{1}{d}\sum^{d}_{i=1}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}^{2}_{0,i}] the average of expected second moment of the individual data components of 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}. By Cheybyshev’s inequality, we can establish the convergence in probability of ‖𝐱0‖2d\frac{||\mathbf{x}_{0}||^{2}}{d} to CC. For any δ>0\delta>0:

P⁡(|‖𝐱0‖2d−C|>δ)\displaystyle P\left(\left|\frac{||\mathbf{x}_{0}||^{2}}{d}-C\right|>\delta\right) ≤1d2​δ2​O​(d)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{d^{2}\delta^{2}}O(d)
∴P⁡(|‖𝐱0‖2d−C|>δ)\displaystyle\therefore P\left(\left|\frac{||\mathbf{x}_{0}||^{2}}{d}-C\right|>\delta\right) →0​ as ​d→∞.\displaystyle\to 0\text{ as }d\to\infty.

If the data distribution is normalized such that its individual components have zero mean and unit variance, then C=1C=1. In this regime, the existence of the mapping μd\mu_{d} does not guarantee the recovery of α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} from 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} as Hd​(𝐱t)H_{d}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) will converge to a constant function. Consequently, this particular mechanism does not guarantee redundancy of the time signal in the loss function.

We can interpret Theorem 3.2 as follows: in high-dimensional spaces, the norm of the corrupted sample 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} concentrates around a deterministic function of α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} whenever the empirical second moment of the components of 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} concentrates around a constant C≠1C\neq 1. Thus, by measuring the norm of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}, we can recover α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} with high probability. The mapping μd\mu_{d} is a theoretical construct to establish existence; in practice, a network may infer the timestep implicitly without needing explicit computation of HdH_{d}.

4 Related Work

Diffusion models [23] adopt an idea from physics, where a sample is gradually converted into a well-known distribution (e.g., Gaussian) by adding noise in a forward process. Then, a reverse process is learned to restore the original data from the noise. In DDPM [6], the reverse process is parameterized by a neural network ϵθ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta} that takes as input the noisy image 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and the temporal signal tt to predict the noise ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon} used to corrupt the original image 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}. To inject the scalar tt into the model, DDPM uses positional encodings followed by a feedforward network. In contrast, DiT [17] uses an AdaIN [7] to inject the time signal into the model.

Various works have explored improving the scheduling of noise scales in diffusion models [16, 10], but the question of whether the time signal itself is necessary has not been thoroughly investigated. Our work fills this gap by providing both theoretical insight and empirical evidence on the redundancy of timestep embeddings in diffusion models.

Denoising Autoencoders (DAE) [28] and Generalized DAEs (GDAE) [1] established early on that generative density modeling can be achieved through iterative corruption-reversal processes without strictly requiring explicit scale or corruption inputs, as exemplified by the Walkback algorithm. Furthermore, Denoising Score Matching (DSM) [29] proved that the DAE objective is equivalent to estimating the score function ∇𝐱t​log​p​(𝐱t)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p(\mathbf{x}_{t}) under a specific noise distribution. This fundamental connection directly underpins Noise Conditional Score Networks (NCSN) [25].

Rooted in these classical foundations, several recent studies have begun to question the strict necessity of explicit timestep conditioning [19, 27, 22, 30], proposing instead modern noise-agnostic or blind denoising frameworks. For instance, [26] establishes general error bounds for time-agnostic generative modeling, while [20] investigates the geometry of diffusion via the marginal energy landscape. Concurrently, [9] leverages the mathematical “blessings of dimensionality” under low intrinsic dimensions or single-data-point assumptions to bypass explicit conditioning.

While these foundational and recent works explore the broad feasibility of noise-agnostic architectures, they predominantly rely on global concentration statistics and fall short in regimes where global features become uninformative. In contrast, our work provides a distinct, complementary perspective through an architectural and local statistical lens. We explicitly analyze normalized latent spaces—a regime where global statistics fail (C≈1C\approx 1)—and prove that noise scale identification remains viable under a weak dependence condition (∑i<j|Cov​(𝐱0,i2,𝐱0,j2)|=O⁡(d)\sum_{i<j}|\text{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{0,i}^{2},\mathbf{x}_{0,j}^{2})|=O(d)) that rigorously accounts for the structural, local nature of spatial image data.

5 Experiments

In this section, we conduct an analysis of timestep embeddings in both U-Net and DiT architectures. We evaluate the impact of removing timestep embeddings on the quality of generated samples using standard metrics such as FID, Precision, and Recall. We also provide a qualitative comparison of the generated images to visually assess the differences in fidelity and diversity between models with and without timestep conditioning.

Experimental Setup

We adopt the common setup for measuring the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [5], following the standard procedure in the literature [6, 11]. For sample diversity and fidelity, we also report Precision and Recall metrics [13]. The setup for Precision and Recall is the same as in [13]. We train on the CelebA dataset with samples at 128×128128\times 128 resolution, and we train on the CIFAR-10 dataset with samples at 32×3232\times 32 resolution. For each dataset, we train two configurations for each architecture: one with timestep embeddings and another without them. For sampling time, we use the clock time when generating 100100 batches of 100100 samples each, and report the average time per batch along with the standard deviation across batches on a RTX 4070 GPU.

Training Details

The U-Net architecture is based on DDPM [6], while the DiT architecture follows the DiT-S/2 configuration of [17] with 252252 hidden units. For the CelebA dataset, we first train a VAE [12] to learn a lower-dimensional latent representation of the data. Then we train both U-Net and DiT in this latent space. For the CIFAR-10 dataset, we directly train both architectures in the data space. The diffusion model in CelebA is conducted in the latent space of the VAE, at 16×1616\times 16 resolution. While in CIFAR-10, it is performed in the data space, at 32×3232\times 32 resolution.

5.1 Quantitative Results

The quantitative results are summarized in Tab. 1 and Tab. 2. In the CelebA dataset, DiT* (DiT without timestep embeddings) achieves an FID of 70.4870.48, which is slightly lower than the 70.0470.04 obtained by standard DiT. In terms of Precision and Recall, DiT* shows a minor decrease in Precision but an improvement in Recall. For U-Net, removal of timestep embeddings leads to a significant improvement in FID from 69.8269.82 to 63.6363.63, as well as increases in both Precision and Recall.

In the CIFAR-10 dataset, the impact of removing timestep embeddings is even more pronounced. DiT* achieves a substantial improvement in FID from 51.3251.32 to 34.7434.74, along with increases in both Precision and Recall. Similarly, U-Net* shows a significant improvement in FID from 52.6752.67 to 41.1841.18, Precision from 0.660.66 to 0.680.68, and Recall from 0.450.45 to 0.570.57. In summary, the quantitative results indicate that removing timestep embeddings can lead to similar performance in terms of FID, Precision, and Recall in the CelebA dataset, while it can lead to significant improvements in these metrics in the CIFAR-10 dataset.

5.2 Qualitative Analysis

The qualitative comparison in Fig. 1 reveals that for the CelebA dataset, both DiT and U-Net generate visually coherent faces with and without timestep embeddings. However, samples from default DiT and U-Net (with timestep embeddings) exhibit fewer artifacts. In contrast, DiT* and U-Net* show a greater diversity in terms of facial features, color distribution, and pose, which may contribute to improved FID scores. In the CIFAR-10 dataset, the differences in Fig. 2 are more difficult to discern visually, but the samples of DiT* and U-Net* appear to have more varied textures and colors, reflecting the redundancy of the temporal signal in guiding the generation process in a high-diversity dataset.

5.3 Robustness and Performance Trade-offs

In terms of computational performance, Tab. 1 shows that removal of timestep embeddings leads to a reduction in inference time for both DiT and U-Net. This suggests that, when the diffusion process is performed in the latent space at 16×1616\times 16 resolution, the temporal conditioning mechanism introduces additional computational overhead, and its removal can lead to more efficient sampling without compromising the quality of generated samples. In the CIFAR-10 dataset, Tab. 2 shows a less pronounced reduction in inference time when removing timestep embeddings, which may be due to the fact that the diffusion process is performed in the data space at 32×3232\times 32 resolution, where the computational overhead of temporal conditioning may be less significant. The performance trade-offs between visual fidelity, diversity, and computational efficiency highlight the potential benefits of re-evaluating the necessity of timestep embeddings in diffusion models.

6 Discussion

Tab. 1 shows a slight decrease in FID for DiT* compared to DiT, accompanied by a minor decrease in Precision and slight increase in Recall. This suggests that timestep embeddings may have a limited role in guiding the denoising process. In contrast, the improvement in FID for U-Net* relative to U-Net indicates that timestep embeddings may be less beneficial—and potentially even detrimental—for convolutional architectures on this dataset. Qualitative analysis in Fig. 1 supports this interpretation, as U-Net* samples exhibit more diversity in facial features and poses, which may contribute to improved FID scores.

In the CIFAR-10 dataset, substantial improvements in FID for both DiT* and U-Net* compared to their standard counterparts indicate that timestep embeddings may not provide additional benefit for conditional image generation in a high-diversity dataset. The increases in both Precision and Recall further indicate that removing timestep embeddings allows the models to generate samples that are not only more diverse but also more representative of the true data distribution. Qualitative analysis supports these interpretations. Samples from DiT* and U-Net* appear to preserve structural details and varied textures. Although the visual differences may be subtle as CIFAR-10 is more diverse and has lower resolution than CelebA, the improved FID scores imply that the models without timestep embeddings are better at capturing the underlying data distribution, leading to an overall improvement in sample quality.

Furthermore, the sampling time results indicate that removing timestep embeddings leads to a reduction in inference time for both DiT and U-Net across both datasets. This suggests that the temporal conditioning mechanism introduces additional computational overhead. The performance trade-offs between visual fidelity, diversity, and computational efficiency highlight the potential benefits of re-evaluating the necessity of timestep embeddings in diffusion models.

Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 provide a theoretical framework for analyzing the potential redundancy of timestep embeddings in diffusion models. In particular, the existence of a measurable mapping μ\mu capable of recovering α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} from the corrupted input. This suggests that, under suitable conditions, a neural network may implicitly infer the noise level without the timestep signal. This occurs when the per-component second moment of the data distribution concentrates around a constant C≠1C\neq 1. In the case of CIFAR-10, diffusion is performed directly in the data space, where CC is not necessarily equal to one. This may partially explain the performance improvements observed when removing timestep embeddings. In contrast, in the CelebA dataset, the diffusion process is conducted in the latent space of a VAE, where samples are normalized to have approximately unit variance across dimensions. In this regime, the mechanism described in Theorem 3.2 may be weakened, which could account for the more limited impact of removing timestep embeddings, especially for the DiT architecture.

The structural resilience of the time-agnostic U-Net* compared to its DiT* counterpart, as evidenced in Tab. 1, can be explained through the lens of Local Identifiability. While Theorem 3.2 establishes that global noise-scale recovery is theoretically constrained in normalized latent spaces where Cglobal≈1C_{\text{global}}\approx 1, natural spatial inhomogeneity ensures that localized sub-structures frequently deviate from unity (Clocal≠1C_{\text{local}}\neq 1).

The capacity to exploit these local variance fluctuations depends heavily on the architecture’s inductive bias and sampling density. A Vision Transformer backbone, such as the DiT, partitions the input into NN sparse, non-overlapping patches, making it statistically more likely to average out spatial sub-structures. Conversely, a convolutional U-Net employing stride-1 convolutions processes the spatial grid as a highly dense set of ≈p2​N​(p>1)\approx p^{2}N\;(p>1) overlapping receptive fields. This sliding-window mechanism dramatically maximizes the empirical probability of encountering localized regions where the noise scale α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} remains identifiable. Consequently, this structural sampling disparity enables CNN-based backbones to maintain robust time-agnostic convergence even within normalized latent manifolds, whereas non-overlapping attention grids suffer a noticeable performance degradation. This architectural insight underscores the critical interplay between model design and the theoretical conditions for timestep redundancy, suggesting that convolutional architectures may be inherently better suited to leverage local identifiability in high-dimensional generative modeling tasks.

7 Conclusion

This work has investigated the role of timestep embeddings in diffusion models, providing both theoretical insights and empirical evidence for their redundancy in high-dimensional regimes. Our theoretical framework demonstrates that the temporal signal is not strictly necessary to guide the denoising process, as the noise scale α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} remains asymptotically identifiable through the corrupted input 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} under certain conditions. Quantitative and qualitative results across the CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets support these findings, showing that time-agnostic models can maintain—and in some cases, surpass—the performance of their conditioned counterparts while reducing computational overhead. While our study is focused on low-to-medium resolution dataset, the scalability to higher resolution synthesis and more complex datasets remains to be verified. Future work should explore these frontiers to determine if timestep embeddings become necessary as data complexity and resolution increase.
